senses: The ceremony of washing the feet of poor persons or inferiors, performed as a religious rite on Maundy Thursday in commemoration of Christ's washing the disciples' feet at the Last Supper.
The office appointed to be read during the religious ceremony of foot-washing.
ety: From Middle English maundee, maunde, from Old French mandée (“mandated”), from Latin mandatum (“commandment”). Doublet of mandate. The word came to refer to the foot-washing ceremony performed on Thursday before Easter because of the phrase used by Jesus to explain his act of foot-washing, which in the Latin Vulgate begins: Mandatum novum do vobis ut diligatis invicem ..., i.e. "A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another …" (John 13:34).

senses: Evil or wicked character or behaviour.
A wicked or treacherous act.
ety: From Middle English vileinie, vileynye, from Anglo-Norman vilenie, from Old French vilanie.
examples: Mos Eisley spaceport- you will never find a more wretched hive of scum and villainy. We must be cautious.

senses: Conversion of a non-passive dynamical system into a passive one.
A Mexican unit of weight for ore, varying from 1,800 to 3,200 Spanish pounds.
A bromine atom.
ety: From obsolete English brome + -ine, this word being from French brome, from Ancient Greek βρῶμος (brômos, “stink”).

senses: Of colours, to be very bright; to be so bright as to appear to radiate as a light source.
A dragonet, a fish of families Callionymidae or Draconettidae.
A Guinea worm (Filaria medinensis, now Dracunculus medinensis).
ety: Borrowed from Latin dracunculus, diminutive of draco (“dragon”).

senses: A textphone.
ety: From a trademark of Ultratec, Inc., possibly from mini- + communicator.
examples: Eventually the trust agreed to install minicoms in all key access points and to make mobile minicoms available to inpatients.
Facilities (eg minicoms, hearing loops, etc.) may be inadequate or staff may be unaware of how to use them.

ety: Borrowed from Italian serenata. Doublet of serenade.
examples: More’s the pity, for this work (technically a serenata) is a little gem, and Aulos polished it to a fine luster.

senses: A robot or artificial being that is an exact copy of a genuine lifeform, especially a human.
ety: From Latin replicāns, present participle of replicō. The science fiction sense was coined by David Peoples in the 1982 film Blade Runner.

senses: A chief (particularly Zulu).
ety: Borrowed from Zulu ínkôsi (“chief, king”), from Proto-Bantu *nkócì (“lion”). Doublet of kgosi.
examples: Before leaving his house to go to the kraal the inkosi had to eat a little porridge.

senses: An apparatus for the separation of dry comminuted ore, by exposing it to intermittent puffs of air.
title of the Venetian envoy to particularly the Sublime Porte
ety: From Venetan bailo. Doublet of bailiff.
examples: Venice engaged to restore to the triarchs all property which the baili had conferred in fief since 1255.
In 1670 the bailo was considered responsible for all the Venetian consuls in the Ottoman Empire.

senses: A French dessert made by piling profiteroles and other crunchy sweets in a tall shape, then pouring caramel over them to hold them in place.
A tracksuit.
examples: Dylan was wearing a light trackie top in the colours of the flag.
Carriages crammed with more sportswear than JD, including what looks like an orange and black trackie, similar to Casey′s; some dad out with his kid. You get a better class of person in Wembley.
Pulling on a pair of trackie pants and a jumper, she quietly unclipped the flyscreen and pushed up the old window and climbed through, landing outside with a hollow thud.

examples: Plays can be televised and have the same appeal as other teledramas.

senses: A door or partition consisting of a wooden frame covered in rice paper, used in traditional Japanese architecture.
In harness racing, a horse with a gait in which the front and back legs on opposite sides take a step together alternating with the other set of opposite legs; as opposed to a pacer.
The foot of a pig, sheep, or other quadruped, especially when prepared as meat.
A tailor's assistant who goes around to receive orders.
ety: From Middle English trottere, equivalent to trot + -er.
examples: Finally Napoleon raised his trotter for silence and announced that he had already made all the arrangements.
In Persia, newly married couples were presented with sheep's trotters steeped in vinegar as a love enticement.

ety: From Hindi सुरमा (surmā) / Urdu سرمہ (surmā), from Classical Persian سرمه (surma).

ety: Borrowed from Middle French sciatique, from Late Latin sciaticus, variant of ischiadicus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Spanish colectivo. In reference to shared taxis, clipping of taxi colectivo. Doublet of collective.

ety: From Japanese 薙刀 (naginata, literally “mowing hatchet”).
